name: CMSIS-DSP (FFT)
baseline: Numerical Recipes in C radix-2 float FFT (textbook plain C); for Q31 a 32-bit adaptation of a textbook fixed-point radix-2 FFT
workload: Complex FFT at several sizes on a Cortex-M4F microcontroller: CMSIS-DSP float32 and Q31 FFT against textbook plain-C FFTs of the same O(n log n) class, with the FPU enabled and disabled for the float case.
claimed_speedup: Float32 FFT about 35x faster than the Numerical Recipes radix-2 FFT with the FPU enabled for both, and about 4x faster on average with the FPU disabled; Q31 FFT about 1.9x faster at every size tested. Figures taken from a search-result summary of the post (page not opened).
compiler_and_flags: Keil MDK 4.70a per a search-result summary of the post; optimisation flags not stated
hardware: STM32F407 (Cortex-M4F) at 30 MHz, zero flash wait states
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; ships in CMSIS packs and has Zephyr integration files in the repo
tradeoffs: Targets Arm Cortex-M (and Neon on Cortex-A); the README says best speed needs -O3 -ffast-math, that GCC currently gives poor Helium code so the Arm compiler is advised, and that -fno-builtin badly hurts the memcpy-based type punning. The docs note some algorithms give slightly different results on different architectures (M0, M4/M7, M55) as a speed trade-off.
caveats: Evidence is a search-result summary of an Arm Community blog post from November 2013 written by an Arm intern (first-party). The page could not be opened from this container (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the benchmark code, flags and per-size tables were not seen. It measures CMSIS-DSP 1.x on one STM32F407 with Keil MDK, and the baselines are unoptimised textbook FFTs, not a tuned C library such as KissFFT. The repo publishes no timings itself: Testing/ holds a cycle-count benchmark framework (desc.txt, bench.txt, summaryBench.py) without committed results, and Documentation/Doxygen/src has no numbers. Counter-evidence that was opened: IAR's wiki measured arm_sqrt_f32 at 14 cycles against sqrtf at 17 on Cortex-M4 and M7 (about 1.2x, derived from page data) but 252 against 229 on a Cortex-M3 without FPU (IAR Embedded Workbench, flags not stated, breakpoint timing); GitHub issue 70 reports the Neon arm_biquad_cascade_df2T_f32 about 80% slower than the reporter's plain optimised C on Cortex-A57 (GCC 7.3, -Ofast), left open as an enhancement. A search summary of a 2013 forum post (not opened) said sinf() ran about 20% faster than arm_sin_f32 on a Cortex-M4F. The win therefore depends strongly on core, FPU, function and compiler.
found_via: seed-record pass starting from https://github.com/ARM-software/CMSIS-DSP; README, Testing/ and Documentation/Doxygen/src had no published timings, so a WebSearch for CMSIS-DSP versus plain-C FFT cycles surfaced the Arm Community blog post 'ARM DSP is the way to go - An intern's perspective' (summary only); the IAR-CMSIS-DSP wiki page and issue 70 were opened for counter-evidence

name: std::atomic counter (fetch_add, relaxed) against a std::mutex-guarded counter (Asynchronous Programming with C++ companion code)
baseline: std::mutex lock/unlock around a shared uint32_t counter increment
workload: Several threads each increment one shared counter hundreds of millions of times (200 million per thread in the book's Table 5.1 at 1, 2 and 4 threads), timed with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock; the checked-in file runs 4 threads.
claimed_speedup: Book Table 5.1, relayed by the seed lead and not present on the repo page: atomic counter 0.82 s, 4.52 s and 9.13 s against mutex 1.03 s, 10.15 s and 24.61 s at one, two and four threads, about 1.3x, 2.2x and 2.7x faster (derived from those book figures).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the table. Root CMakeLists.txt adds -O3 -DNDEBUG only for CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and sets no default build type; README lists GCC 14.2, Clang 18, Boost 1.86, C++20/23 on Ubuntu 24.04.
tradeoffs: A single shared counter only: an atomic does not protect multi-step critical sections, and relaxed ordering gives no ordering with other variables. The gap is for a maximal-contention microbenchmark with no work between increments.
caveats: The book's timings are first-party and are not in the repo (no results file); no CPU, compiler version or flags are given with them. The checked-in Chapter_05/5x01-atomic_flag.cpp does not reproduce the table as described: it fixes 4 threads and runs 200000000 iterations per thread for the mutex variant but 500000000 for the spinlock and atomic variants, so its printed times are not like-for-like; it also lacks #include <mutex>. Release flags apply only if the user selects the Release build type. The latest commit (2026-04-22) is titled 'remove expired conference banner', so recent activity looks like repository upkeep rather than code work (code-change dates not checked). Not compared against other mutex or lock implementations.

name: alignas(64) per-thread result slots against false sharing (Asynchronous Programming with C++ companion code)
baseline: adjacent unpadded 8-byte per-thread result slots (false sharing on one cache line)
workload: Eight pinned std::thread workers each draw 100 million std::mt19937 values through uniform_int_distribution(1,5) and add them to a per-thread unsigned long slot; slots packed adjacently against slots in structs aligned with alignas(64); wall clock with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock.
claimed_speedup: Book, relayed by the seed lead and not present on the repo page: 4403 ms with adjacent slots against 160 ms aligned to 64 bytes, about 27x (ratio 27.5x derived from those figures); the book also reports perf stat cache misses of 96.63% against 27.21%.
compiler_and_flags: Chapter_13/CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++20 -march=native; the repo README lists GCC 14.2 and Clang 18, while the lead says GCC (13) with libstdc++ produced the numbers.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper Pro 5975WX, Ubuntu 24.04 (from the book via the seed lead; the repo itself does not state a CPU)
tradeoffs: Each slot grows from 8 to 64 bytes. The alignment is hard-coded to 64 rather than std::hardware_destructive_interference_size, so it is wrong for CPUs with 128-byte destructive interference (some Arm and Apple cores). Pinning uses pthread_setaffinity_np, so the code is Linux-only.
caveats: First-party book numbers; the benchmark code and CMake flags are public but the CPU model and the results exist only in the book, so this is tier C, not A. The checked-in main() runs only the aligned variant (the unaligned call is commented out). Single run. Slots are plain non-atomic stores, so how much false sharing occurs also depends on whether the compiler keeps the accumulator in a register. Threads are pinned to cores 0-7 of a many-core CPU, and the effect size depends on the cache topology. The comparison is an idiom difference (padded against packed slots), not a library against the standard library.

name: SPSC lock-free ring buffer with cached head and tail indices (Asynchronous Programming with C++ companion code)
baseline: the book's own power-of-two SPSC ring buffer without cached head/tail copies (head_ and tail_ atomics on separate 64-byte-aligned slots); not Boost.Lockfree, not a mutex-guarded std::queue
workload: One producer thread (core 2) pushes and one consumer thread (core 12) pops 1 billion ints through a 2^17-element queue; the consumer checks the order; operations per second = iterations divided by wall time.
claimed_speedup: Book, relayed by the seed lead and not present on the repo page: about 101.6 million to about 162.5 million ops/sec, roughly 60% faster (1.6x); perf stat cache misses 41.30% down to 31.39%.
compiler_and_flags: Chapter_13/CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++20 -march=native; README lists GCC 14.2 and Clang 18, the lead says GCC 13 was used.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper Pro 5975WX, Ubuntu 24.04 (from the book via the seed lead; the repo itself does not state a CPU)
tradeoffs: Single-producer single-consumer only; capacity must be a power of two and one slot stays unused; the element type must be default-constructible and copy-assignable; both sides busy-spin when the queue is empty or full; it uses plain std::vector storage with no padding between buffer slots.
caveats: Comparison is between two variants of the book's own queue, so there is no standard-library, Boost.Lockfree, rigtorp SPSCQueue or mutex-queue baseline. Numbers are first-party and not in the repo; the CPU model exists only in the book, so tier C. Core ids 2 and 12 are specific to the author's machine and map to different cache domains elsewhere. The two classes also differ in member layout, which the benchmark does not isolate: alignas(64) on head_ and tail_ does not pad the members that follow, so in the baseline capacity_ and the buffer pointer share tail_'s cache line, while in the optimised class they follow cache_tail_ instead (my reading of the source, effect not measured). Single run.

name: Direct-indexed std::array maps in the matching-engine order book (Building Low Latency Applications with C++ companion code)
baseline: std::unordered_map (nested std::unordered_map<ClientId, std::unordered_map<OrderId, MEOrder*>> and std::unordered_map<Price, MEOrdersAtPrice*> in UnorderedMapMEOrderBook)
workload: 100,000 pre-generated client requests (alternating NEW and CANCEL of a random earlier order, prices within 10 ticks of a random base) applied to one limit order book; RDTSC cycles around each add() and cancel() call; MEOrderBook (std::array maps indexed by order id and price modulo 256) against UnorderedMapMEOrderBook, which differs only in those two map members.
claimed_speedup: Book, relayed by the seed lead and not present on the repo page: 142650 RDTSC cycles per operation with array maps against 152457 with std::unordered_map, i.e. the unordered_map version about 6 to 7% slower (array version about 1.07x faster, derived).
compiler_and_flags: g++ pinned in CMakeLists.txt (README lists GCC 11.3.0), -std=c++2a -Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wpedantic, built by scripts/build.sh with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default Release flags -O3 -DNDEBUG). libstdc++ is inferred from g++ on Linux.
hardware: four-core ThinkPad X1 Carbon laptop at about 2.6 GHz (from the book via the seed lead; CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Direct indexing needs bounded dense ids and compile-time sizes (ME_MAX_NUM_CLIENTS 256 x ME_MAX_ORDER_IDS 1048576 pointers is about 2 GiB per order book, trading memory for no hashing and no allocation; the price index is price modulo ME_MAX_PRICE_LEVELS (256) in both book variants).
caveats: First-party book numbers; benchmark source, compiler and build script are public but the CPU model is not and the results are not in the repo, so tier C. The two books share one matching engine and are run back to back in one process, single run (the lead says results vary between runs). The per-operation cost of over 100000 cycles shows the timed add() and cancel() are dominated by other work (matching and logging), so the map difference is a small slice. The harness divides the total by loop_count * 2 although only loop_count calls are timed, so the printed cycles are half the true per-call average; the ratio is unaffected. The comparison is an idiom difference (preallocated array against node-based std::unordered_map), not a library; the unordered_map variant also adds a find() in a lookup path. Category changed from the assigned allocators because the measured baseline is std::unordered_map.
